subject: Continuous piecewise-linear fit with inferred knots

messages.author: 5e455894088e20d6
messages.subject: Continuous piecewise-linear fit with inferred knots
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to fit a continuous piecewise linear curve to a short time-series. I know that there will be three pieces to the curve, with different gradients; that the first gradient is negative; the second is near zero; the third is positive. The time-series can be fairly varied, but the extrema look like these two :

http://i.stack.imgur.com/AgCGD.png
http://i.stack.imgur.com/ohw6Q.png

I'm trying to infer the location of the knots using PyStan, as well as the gradients of the lines and the intercept. Here's my code :


model_code = """
    data {
        int <lower = 0> N; // length of time series
        real <lower = 0> C[N]; // time series
    }
    
    parameters {
        real <lower = 1, upper = N-1> t1; // first knot
        real <lower = t1, upper = N> t2; // second knot
        real <upper = -1> m1; // down-stroke gradient
        real m2; // gradient at minimum
        real <lower = 1> m3; // up-stroke gradient
        real <lower = 0> c; // intercept
    }
    
    model {
        int tt1; // first knot index
        int tt2; // second knot index
        vector[N] mu; // continuous piecewise-linear regression line
        
        tt1 <- 1; // this doesn't work with = ?
        tt2 <- 2; // anyway, initiate the indices
        
        // and "typecast" the inferred knot reals to ints
        while ((tt1 + 1) < floor(t1)) {
            tt1 <- tt1 + 1;
        }
        
        while ((tt2 + 1) < floor(t2)) {
            tt2 <- tt2 + 1;
        }
        
        
        // generate piecewise line
        for (i in 1:tt1) {
            mu[i] <- c + i * m1;
        }
        
        for (i in 1:tt2) {
            mu[i] <- mu[tt1-1] + i * m2;
        }
        
        for (i in 1:(N-tt2)) {
            mu[i] <- mu[tt2-1] + i * m3;
        }
        
        
        // data is normally distributed around this line
        C ~ normal(mu, 10);
    }
"""


# Data
model_data = { "N" : len(da), "C" : da }

# Initial estimates
init = dict(c = C.max(), t1 = len(C)/4, t2 = 3 * len(C)/4, m1 = -100, m2 = 0, m3 = 100)

# Fit
fit = ps.stan(model_code = model_code, data = model_data, iter = 500, chains = 4, init = init)





If I run the above, I get the error,

ValueError: Invalid specification of initial values.



But I haven't been able to find any docs on how to declare initial values correctly in PyStan.



If I run the above without providing initial values, I get



RuntimeError: Something went wrong after call_sampler.





Any help is much appreciated here ! I'd love to get this code up and running.



Also, the ability to cast a real into a int would be fantastic...



Thanks very much !

Quentin

Dr. Quentin CAUDRON
Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
Princeton University

Apologies, I've identified a few problems in my code at this point. I've also found an old post in this usergroup regarding initialising parameters in PyStan. I recommend that this be put in the manual, if possible - I didn't find it ! For any PyStan users :
def initialisation() :
    return dict(param1 = 42, param2 = 0.53, ...)

and pass "initialisation" to the init argument of stan.sample().


A follow-up question, to ensure this thread doesn't go to waste. The corrected code is below. It doesn't seem to converge, after, say, 5000 samples. This seems fairly slow for what should be a clear(ish) problem. Does anyone have any suggestions on how to obtain this kind of fit, in a faster way ?

Thanks !

model_code = """
    data {
        int <lower = 0> N;

real <lower = 0> C[N];
    }

parameters {
        real <lower = 1, upper = N-1> t1;
real <lower = t1, upper = N> t2;
real <upper = -1> m1; // down-stroke gradient
real m2; // plateau / gradient at minimum

real <lower = 1> m3; // up-stroke gradient
        real <lower = 0> c; // intercept
    }
    
    model {
        int tt1;

int tt2;
        vector[N] mu;
        
        tt1 <- 1;
        tt2 <- 2;

while ((tt1 + 1) < floor(t1)) {
            tt1 <- tt1 + 1;
        }
        
        while ((tt2 + 1) < floor(t2)) {
            tt2 <- tt2 + 1;
        }

for (i in 1:tt1) {
            mu[i] <- c + i * m1;
        }

for (i in 1:(tt2-tt1)) {
            mu[i+tt1] <- mu[tt1-1] + i * m2;

}
        
        for (i in 1:(N-tt2)) {

mu[i+tt2] <- mu[tt2-1] + i * m3;
        }
        
        
        
        C ~ normal(mu, 100);

}
"""

model_data = { "N" : len(da), "C" : da }

def initial() :
    return dict(t1 = len(da)/4, t2 = 3 * len(da)/4, m1 = -100, m2 = 0, m3 = 100, c = da.max())


fit = ps.stan(model_code = model_code, data = model_data, iter = 5000, chains = 4, init = initial)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Continuous piecewise-linear fit with inferred knots
parts:
Thanks for your replies, Michael and Kenneth. 

What I'm really after are these switchpoints. The plots are actually the times between two epidemics. At t_0, we're at the height of the first epidemic, and at t_end, the peak of the next epidemic. What we're trying to infer is the time that the last epidemic ends ( first switchpoint ), and the time when the second one begins ( switchpoint two ). For the second graph, it's extremely clear, but for the first one, we continue to see some infected individuals, and so it's harder to say when one ends and the other begins. The model I've chosen assumes that the epidemics have a "downswing", a time where the number of infecteds are more or less constant, and an upswing to the next epidemic. I'm looking for the times when the changes occur.

I haven't considered Gaussian processes for this situation, but I'll look into it. Thanks for the recommendation !

Otherwise though - a discontinuous gradient will giving long mixing times, is that correct ?

Thanks again.
Quentin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Continuous piecewise-linear fit with inferred knots
parts:
Yes, discontinuous gradients are bad for HMC.  A GP would be nice, but perhaps you could also looking into a mixture model, with separate downswing, constant, and upswing components?  So long as each component is smooth the mixture will be smooth, and
you can model the relative phases (as a proxy for switchpoints) no problem.

Thanks for your replies, Michael and Kenneth. 

What I'm really after are these switchpoints. The plots are actually the times between two epidemics. At t_0, we're at the height of the first epidemic, and at t_end, the peak of the next epidemic. What we're trying to infer is the time that the last epidemic ends ( first switchpoint ), and the time when the second one begins ( switchpoint two ). For the second graph, it's extremely clear, but for the first one, we continue to see some infected individuals, and so it's harder to say when one ends and the other begins. Quentin

Be careful with these models — if the gradient is not continuous there’s
no guarantee the Hamiltonian transitions will be accurate and give you
efficient sampling.

    return dict(t1 = len(da)/4, t2 = 3 * len(da)/4, m1 = -100, m2 = 0, m3 = 100, c = da.max())

parts:
Quentin,

I was thinking about something simple (at least to start).  If you have approximate shapes for
the three phases (upswing, meta-equilibrium, downswing) then you could fit the model as
a sum of the three shapes with their relative offsets in time and magnitudes free parameters.
Then the cut points can be computed as the locations where one component rises past 
another (computable analytically for many possible shapes).

Not sure how easy it would be to model those shapes, but it seems more informative than
fitting with a non-parameteric model and simply looking for the changes in derivative.

Cool.  The other advantage with an approach like this is that you can put lots of science into the model, for example modeling an epidemic with a Gaussian or a Laplacian and then modeling with a mixture of two of these guys and a uniform between them.
In fact, if you assumed that data collection started in the midst of one epidemic and ended in the midst of another your model would be two exponentials decaying from the boundaries and uniform in between, very similar to the simple piecewise linear
model you have used here.

Good luck!
